narrative:
The model estimated a 56.1% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is above a coin flip, so the school treated it as sufficient risk to deny your application. This is a probability, not a certainty: the model still gives you roughly a 44% chance of passing.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class-rank decile, which was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your value of 1 is far from the average of about 5.8 among accepted students. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.40, which worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, since it is above the accepted-student average of about 3.23. The third factor was your first-year class-rank decile, also 1, compared with an accepted-student average near 6; it again pushed the prediction toward failure. Overall, the two class-rank signals outweighed the positive GPA signal.

Next, ask admissions whether you can submit a reconsideration statement or reapply with new evidence. Consider retaking the LSAT—your 29.5 is below the accepted average of about 37.2—and provide an academic support plan, updated letters, or work and study experience that shows readiness for law school and bar preparation. Because the prediction is probabilistic, context and improvement can matter.
